segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who are under the yoke as slaves must regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be slandered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those whose masters are believers must not look down on them because they are brothers; rather, they must serve them all the more, because those who benefit from their good service are believers and beloved. Teach these things and urge them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone teaches otherwise and does not hold to healthy words, those of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the teaching that accords with godliness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing, but is sick with a craving for disputes and battles over words. From these come envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and constant wrangling among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a way to profit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Godliness with contentment is in fact a way to great profit;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for we brought nothing into the world, and neither can we carry anything out of it;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare and many senseless and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the love of money is the root of all evils, and some, in reaching for it, have been led astray from the faith and have pierced themselves with many pains.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, O man of God, flee these things, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Contend in the good contest of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and for which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his witness before Pontius Pilate made the good confession,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to keep the commandment spotless and beyond reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which the blessed and only Sovereign will display in its own time—the King of those who reign as kings and Lord of those who rule as lords,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no human being has seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal might. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Charge those who are rich in the present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, turning away from the profane empty talk and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which some have professed and so have missed the mark regarding the faith. Grace be with you.

notes.phrase: those who benefit from their good service
notes.traditional: those who benefit by their good service
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'those who take hold of the good deed'. Most interpreters take this as the masters who receive the slaves' service, which strikingly casts the slave as the benefactor. The phrase can also mean 'those who devote themselves to doing good', describing the masters as benefactors; the grammar allows either.

The traditional 'sound' hides a medical metaphor. The Greek word means 'to be in good health', and the next verse sets it against a teacher who is 'sick' with a craving for disputes. 'Healthy' keeps the contrast the author built.

The word was a favourite of Stoic and Cynic philosophers, for whom it meant self-sufficiency: needing nothing beyond what one has. Here it is given a religious setting, and the related verb appears in verse 8 ('we will be content'). The same Greek word for 'a way to profit' is used in verses 5 and 6, so the author is turning the opponents' own claim back on them.

notes.traditional: and we cannot take anything out
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts join the two clauses with a word that normally means 'because' or 'that', which is awkward here. Later copyists smoothed it by adding 'it is clear that' or 'it is true that'. Most translations, like this one, treat the connection as loose; some take it as 'so that' or 'just as'.

notes.traditional: a root of all kinds of evil
notes.note: The Greek has no article before 'root', so it can be read as 'a root' or 'the root'; a predicate noun placed before the verb often lacks the article even when definite. The following phrase is plainly 'all evils', which most modern versions soften to 'all kinds of evil'. The sentence has the form of a proverb, and Greek moralists had similar sayings; such maxims state things absolutely without claiming there are no exceptions.

The noun and its verb ordinarily refer to an athletic contest, such as a race or a wrestling or boxing match, and by extension to any strenuous struggle. 'Fight the good fight' suggests warfare to a modern reader, which is not the usual picture. 'Contend' and 'contest' also preserve the Greek's repetition of one word-family.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, different in kind as well as unending. The chapter plays on this: the rich are rich 'in the present age' (verse 17) and are urged to take hold of 'the life that is truly life' (verse 19).

The preposition can mean 'in the presence of', as of someone appearing before a magistrate, or 'in the time of'. The first is chosen because it parallels Timothy's own confession 'in the presence of many witnesses'. On the second reading the phrase would refer to Jesus' whole witness, including his death, under Pilate's governorship.

notes.phrase: the King of those who reign as kings and Lord of those who rule as lords
notes.traditional: the King of kings and Lord of lords
notes.note: The Greek here does not use the nouns 'kings' and 'lords', as Revelation does, but participles: those who are reigning and those who are ruling. The traditional wording assimilates this verse to the more familiar title. The meaning is much the same, with the emphasis on those who currently hold power.

notes.phrase: what has been entrusted to you
notes.traditional: that which is committed to thy trust; the deposit
notes.note: The word is a legal and commercial term for property left in another person's keeping, which the keeper was bound to return intact. Here it stands for the teaching Timothy has received and must preserve unaltered.

The opponents evidently claimed a special 'knowledge' (Greek gnosis). The word later gave its name to the movements called Gnostic, but the letter does not give enough detail to identify these teachers with any known later system, and scholars disagree about how far the connection goes. 'Contradictions' may mean their counter-arguments or the self-contradictions of their teaching.

The 'you' is plural in the earliest manuscripts, so a letter addressed to one person closes with a blessing on a wider group, presumably the congregation that would hear it read. Many later manuscripts have the singular, and some add 'Amen'.

candidates.reason: Frequent in the Pastorals, 2 Peter and Acts; 'godliness', 'piety', 'reverence' and 'devotion' are all defensible, and the traditional word is now archaic, so one decision is needed.
Occurs throughout the New Testament and translations vary between 'slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant', both for literal slaves and for metaphorical uses such as 'slave of Christ'.
The medical metaphor ('healthy teaching/words') recurs across all three Pastoral letters, and 'sound' versus 'healthy' should be settled once.
Used of abusive speech against both God and people across the New Testament; whether to use 'blaspheme', 'slander' or 'revile', and when, needs one policy (βλασφημία in v. 4 is rendered 'slander').
A term used for the manifestation of a god or the arrival of a ruler, recurring in the Pastorals and 2 Thessalonians; 'appearing', 'manifestation' and 'epiphany' compete.

warnings: Verse 2: πιστός is not rendered with a register form (faithful / believing) and has no register-exception note.
